active_paradigms.idea: Use exact branch-and-bound with conflict-commutation canonicalization, memoized by functools.lru_cache
active_paradigms.description: The current program is a width-8 prefix beam search: it evaluates every one-transaction extension with the real simulator, retains only eight low-cost prefixes, then reaches a 1-move insertion local optimum. This is strong because it optimizes the actual makespan rather than a length/write-count proxy, but its prefix truncation can permanently discard an order whose early prefix is expensive but whose later conflict overlap is excellent. Replace beam truncation for tractable instances with depth-first branch-and-bound over complete transaction permutations. Treat the current beam-plus-insertion result as the initial incumbent, so pruning begins with a strong upper bound. A partial sequence's simulator makespan is a valid monotone lower bound if adding transactions cannot shorten an already scheduled prefix; prune whenever that lower bound is at least the incumbent. Before branching, identify pairs of remaining transactions that have no read/write conflict on any item and impose a deterministic canonical order on such interchangeable choices, avoiding exploration of equivalent permutations. Use functools.lru_cache for conflict-pair tests and for each evaluated prefix tuple's exact simulator cost. Retain the current beam method only as a time-bounded fallback when the exact search node budget is exceeded.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly minimizes the sole evaluated quantity, the real workload.get_opt_seq_cost makespan, while eliminating the beam's irreversible early-prefix mistakes.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not cache only by the set of selected transactions: different orders of the same set can produce different simulator states and costs. Commutation pruning is safe only when two transactions have no shared key for which at least one access is a write; read/read overlap is nonconflicting. Keep a strict node/time budget and always return the incumbent schedule, because exhaustive search remains factorial on dense large workloads.

active_paradigms.idea: Apply deterministic very-large-neighborhood descent by exhaustively permuting a contiguous transaction window with itertools.permutations
active_paradigms.description: The present insertion phase is already a complete 1-transaction relocation neighborhood, repeated three times, so merely adding swaps or more random restarts is unlikely to escape its local minima; randomized iterated local search was also already unsuccessful. Use a different neighborhood: select a contiguous window of k transactions in the incumbent order, keep all transactions outside the window fixed, and enumerate every ordering of the k removed transactions with itertools.permutations. Score each reconstructed full sequence using workload.get_opt_seq_cost and accept the best strict improvement for that window. A window of 5 has only 120 candidates and a window of 6 has 720, yet it can reverse several mutually conflicting transactions simultaneously, which a monotone insertion descent often cannot do. Sweep windows around high-conflict boundaries first, where adjacent transactions share write-related keys, rather than spending calls on unrelated regions. Continue until one full deterministic sweep produces no improving window; optionally alternate k=5 and k=6 if the evaluation budget permits. This is an exact optimizer over each selected neighborhood and always preserves or improves the current real score.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Escape 1-move insertion local minima caused by coupled conflict chains, using only exact full-schedule makespan evaluations.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not compare partial-window costs: each candidate must be evaluated as the complete order because downstream operation overlap determines the score. Deduplicate candidates when a window contains transactions with identical conflict signatures, and use strict '<' acceptance to avoid cycles and score-noise churn. Cap k conservatively: k=7 already requires 5,040 simulator calls per window.

active_paradigms.idea: Generate a conflict-locality schedule with scipy.sparse.csgraph.reverse_cuthill_mckee as a deterministic independent seed
active_paradigms.description: Current beam construction has very little diversity: all survivors are chosen solely by short-prefix cost, so they commonly collapse into the same region before insertion begins. Construct a sparse undirected transaction conflict matrix whose edge weight is the number of shared keys with at least one write, optionally multiplied by the number of conflicting operation pairs. Call scipy.sparse.csgraph.reverse_cuthill_mckee on this matrix to obtain a transaction order that minimizes the bandwidth of the conflict graph; evaluate both that order and its reversal with the real simulator and retain the better one as an alternative candidate. The structural rationale is that transactions which strongly conflict are brought close in the serial order, reducing long-range chains in which a transaction's late write stalls many otherwise independent operations. This is fundamentally unlike random restart, failed connected-component decomposition, and prefix beam scoring: it uses the global conflict topology in one deterministic graph ordering call. Compare this complete structural schedule directly against the beam-and-insertion output, returning whichever has lower get_opt_seq_cost. If desired, use the graph order as the incumbent for the exact or window optimizer rather than running an additional unrelated heuristic pipeline.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Provides a globally diverse, conflict-aware full permutation that can beat a beam trapped by misleading prefix makespans, while final selection remains based solely on actual makespan.
active_paradigms.cautions: The matrix must include only read/write and write/write relationships; read/read sharing must contribute zero. Reverse Cuthill-McKee operates on a sparse symmetric graph and does not itself know operation timing, so never return it without evaluating its actual simulator cost. Isolated transactions may be ordered arbitrarily and should not be interpreted as dependencies.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace width-8 beam truncation with best-first branch-and-bound over transaction prefixes using heapq
tried_paradigms.description: The current program evaluates true simulator cost for every beam extension, which is valuable, but it irrevocably discards all but eight prefixes based only on their current partial cost. Use a priority queue of prefix states instead: each state contains an ordered prefix, remaining transactions, and `workload.get_opt_seq_cost(prefix)`. This partial cost is a valid lower bound if adding transactions cannot reduce already induced precedence delays, so prune a state whenever its bound is at least the best complete schedule found. Obtain a strong incumbent early from the existing greedy/beam construction, then expand the lowest-bound live state first. Branch transaction choices in an informed order, such as trying extensions with the lowest immediate simulator cost first, so high-quality complete schedules are found early and make pruning effective. For small transaction counts this becomes exact rather than heuristic; for larger instances, impose a node budget and return the best incumbent, which still avoids the arbitrary width-8 failure mode. This directly addresses the main weakness of the current algorithm: two prefixes with similar current cost can have radically different achievable final makespans, yet one is currently discarded permanently.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The returned makespan from `workload.get_opt_seq_cost`; prioritize finding a globally optimal permutation whenever the search tree can be exhausted, while retaining an anytime best schedule under a search budget.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Validate monotonicity of partial-prefix cost before relying on it as a pruning bound; if the simulator's partial cost can decrease after an extension, use it only as a queue priority and do not prune from it. Store immutable tuple prefixes in queue states and use a deterministic tie-break counter because Python cannot compare arbitrary equal-priority state payloads. Set a practical expansion cap for large workloads, since worst-case permutation search remains exponential.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use disconnected conflict-component decomposition with NetworkX before searching orderings
tried_paradigms.description: Build the transaction conflict graph directly from the workload: connect two transactions if they access a common key and at least one access is a write. The present beam search treats every transaction as globally coupled, even though transactions in distinct graph components have no read-write or write-write dependency and therefore their relative order cannot create a conflict edge. Call `networkx.connected_components` on this graph and solve the ordering inside each nontrivial component independently, using an exact search or a substantially wider beam because each subproblem is much smaller. Transactions with no conflict edges may be placed anywhere and should not consume search effort. Concatenate the component schedules in a deterministic order, then evaluate the resulting full schedule once with the real simulator; optionally test the small number of component-order permutations when there are few components, because this is cheap and protects against undocumented simulator behavior. This is fundamentally different from tuning the beam: it reduces the dimension of the actual combinatorial problem by exploiting exact independence. It is especially valuable when workloads are formed from several key clusters, where global factorial search is unnecessary.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan indirectly through exact removal of irrelevant cross-component ordering decisions, allowing much stronger optimization of conflict-dense components within the same evaluation-time budget.
tried_paradigms.cautions: A graph edge must be added only for pairs sharing a key for which at least one transaction writes; read-read sharing is not a conflict. Inspect the available Workload transaction representation carefully and parse operation strings only if no structured operation list is exposed. Do not assume component concatenation is safe without one full-cost check; if simulator semantics include a global resource beyond data conflicts, retain a final cross-component ordering check.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use randomized iterated local search with shuffle-based diverse restarts and full swap/block neighborhoods
tried_paradigms.description: The current code starts from a single narrow-beam solution and accepts only strictly improving one-transaction relocations, so it stops at the first insertion-local optimum. Use `random.shuffle` to generate diverse transaction permutations or diverse tie orders, refine each with simulator-evaluated local search, and retain the best complete schedule across `num_seqs` restarts. Within a restart, evaluate both pairwise swaps and remove-and-reinsert moves; swaps are important because a beneficial exchange can require moving both transactions, while the current first-improvement relocation may require a temporary worsening move and cannot cross that barrier. Use best-improvement selection per local-search pass rather than committing to the first detected improvement, then repeat until neither neighborhood improves. Seed some restarts from the beam solution after a substantial random perturbation, and seed others from completely shuffled schedules, so the search explores both nearby and distant basins. Every acceptance decision must use `workload.get_opt_seq_cost` on the complete candidate, not proxy statistics such as transaction length or write count. This turns `num_seqs` into actual diversification budget and is robust when a full branch-and-bound search is too expensive.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Best complete-schedule makespan over multiple independent local-optimum basins; this specifically targets improvements unavailable to strict single-start insertion descent.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Cache evaluated complete permutation tuples during a restart or globally to avoid repeatedly invoking the simulator for the same swap/insertion result. Keep randomization reproducible with a fixed seed unless the benchmark intentionally rewards stochastic variation. Full swap plus all insertion evaluations cost O(n^3) simulator calls per pass, so cap passes or use candidate lists for very large n; never replace final candidate evaluation with a heuristic estimate.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use exact permutation enumeration for small transaction sets via itertools.permutations
tried_paradigms.description: The current program performs a width-8 beam search using the simulator cost of an incomplete prefix, then applies only three rounds of one-transaction relocation. Its strength is that every retained candidate and every local-search move is evaluated by workload.get_opt_seq_cost, so it optimizes the actual hidden conflict/makespan semantics rather than a proxy. Its major weakness is beam pruning: a prefix with a slightly worse partial cost may enable a much better final interleaving, but is irreversibly discarded before local search begins. Add an exact mode when workload.num_txns is small enough that n! simulator evaluations fit the evaluation budget, for example n <= 9 or a dynamically chosen factorial budget. Enumerate each complete permutation, evaluate workload.get_opt_seq_cost on that complete sequence, and return the best schedule directly. This is fundamentally stronger than any prefix beam because it never assumes that prefix makespan ranks final makespan correctly. Keep the current heuristic only as the fallback for larger n, since the evaluator accepts a schedule and scores it through the actual simulator.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Direct minimization of the hidden evaluator's primary makespan for small workloads; this removes beam-pruning error completely and is deterministic.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The visible evaluator is only a lock-wrapped forwarding function, so no secondary metric or score aggregation is exposed; do not optimize an invented surrogate. Put a strict cap on the number of complete schedules evaluated, since factorial growth is severe. Tie-break equal costs deterministically to avoid run-to-run differences.

tried_paradigms.idea: Solve a direct precedence-and-makespan mixed-integer model with scipy.optimize.milp
tried_paradigms.description: Replace prefix-cost ranking with a single global discrete optimization model whenever the conflict relation can be reconstructed from the transaction operation strings. Create binary precedence variables x[i,j] indicating whether transaction i is before transaction j, impose x[i,j] + x[j,i] = 1, and add triangle/transitivity constraints or an equivalent integer rank variable for each transaction. Build operation start-time variables and a makespan variable C; preserve every operation's within-transaction order and add disjunctive precedence constraints for every cross-transaction read/write or write/write conflict on the same key, gated by the corresponding transaction-order binary. Minimize C with scipy.optimize.milp and then sort transactions by the solved rank variables to produce the required sequence. This directly targets global makespan instead of the current beam's incomplete-prefix cost, and it can retain globally useful choices that local relocation cannot reach. Validate the extracted order once with workload.get_opt_seq_cost; if the simulator’s exact locking semantics differ from the reconstructed constraints, use the solver result as a high-quality initial schedule for the existing exact-cost improvement logic rather than trusting the model’s objective alone. The model is especially promising when conflicts are sparse, because only conflicting operation pairs need constraints.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The actual makespan lower-level precedence structure globally, rather than a heuristic ordering score; potentially proves optimality or provides a strong global lower bound.
tried_paradigms.cautions: This is valid only if Workload exposes or permits parsing transaction operations and its simulator semantics can be modeled faithfully. Big-M constants must be safe but reasonably tight, operation durations must match the simulator, and all conflicting read/write pairs—not read/read pairs—must be represented. Dense workloads can create too many binary variables and constraints, so gate this mode by transaction/operation count and use a solver time limit.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use NetworkX minimum-fill tree decomposition to exploit sparse conflict graph separators
tried_paradigms.description: Construct the undirected transaction conflict graph, with an edge exactly when two transactions access a common key and at least one access is a write. The present beam method treats every remaining transaction as globally coupled, although independent connected components and small graph separators create substantial exact structure. Call networkx.algorithms.approximation.treewidth_min_fill_in to obtain a low-width elimination/decomposition guide for this graph. Use the resulting bags to perform exact dynamic programming over boundary transaction orders: retain only the relative order and simulator-relevant frontier state for transactions crossing a separator, while optimize transactions internal to a bag before forgetting them. At a minimum, disconnected components should be optimized separately and then merged by testing component-level interleavings with actual get_opt_seq_cost; a true decomposition DP extends this benefit to nearly separable sparse graphs. Each completed candidate must still be scored by workload.get_opt_seq_cost, preserving alignment with the hidden evaluator despite the evaluator source itself not being visible beyond the wrapper. This attacks a different weakness from wider beam search: it reduces combinatorial dimension according to actual conflict topology instead of arbitrary beam width.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Makespan on sparse or modular workloads by avoiding needless global permutation search and preserving exact alternatives across small conflict separators.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The minimum-fill decomposition is heuristic and only valuable when the conflict graph has low effective treewidth; dense all-to-all conflict workloads should fall back to direct search. A graph edge must reflect the simulator’s precise conflict definition, including write-write and read-write but excluding read-read. Do not assume independently optimized components can simply be concatenated: test merges with the actual cost oracle because nonconflicting transactions may beneficially overlap.
